How to Work Well on Teams如何在团队中高效协作

Chapter 2. How to Work Well on Teams · 第 2 章 · 如何在团队中高效协作

Written by Brian Fitzpatrick; Edited by Riona MacNamara.

作者：Brian Fitzpatrick；编辑：Riona MacNamara。

Because this chapter is about the cultural and social aspects of software engineering at Google, it makes sense to begin by focusing on the one variable over which you definitely have control: you.

由于本章讨论的是 Google 软件工程中的文化与社会层面，从你唯一确实能掌控的那个变量开始是合理的：你自己。

People are inherently imperfect—we like to say that humans are mostly a collection of intermittent bugs. But before you can understand the bugs in your coworkers, you need to understand the bugs in yourself. We’re going to ask you to think about your own reactions, behaviors, and attitudes—and in return, we hope you gain some real insight into how to become a more efficient and successful software engineer who spends less energy dealing with people-related problems and more time writing great code.

人天生是不完美的——我们喜欢说，人类大体上是一堆间歇性发作的 bug 的集合。但在你能理解同事身上的 bug 之前，你需要先理解自己身上的 bug。我们会请你思考自己的反应、行为与态度——作为回报，我们希望你能获得一些真正的洞见：如何成为一名更高效、更成功的软件工程师，把更少精力花在处理人际问题上，把更多时间用来写出优秀代码。

The critical idea in this chapter is that software development is a team endeavor. And to succeed on an engineering team—or in any other creative collaboration—you need to reorganize your behaviors around the core principles of humility, respect, and trust.

本章的关键思想是：软件开发是一项团队事业。要在一个工程团队里取得成功——或在任何其他创造性协作中——你需要围绕谦逊、尊重与信任这三条核心原则来重塑自己的行为。

Before we get ahead of ourselves, let’s begin by observing how software engineers tend to behave in general.

在展开之前，我们先来观察一下软件工程师通常是如何行事的。

Help Me Hide My Code · 帮我藏起我的代码

For the past 20 years, my colleague Ben and I have spoken at many programming conferences. In 2006, we launched Google’s (now deprecated) open source Project

过去 20 年里，我和同事 Ben 在许多编程大会上做过演讲。2006 年，我们推出了 Google 那个（如今已弃用的）开源项目托管服务，起初我们常收到关于这个产品的许多问题和请求。

原书第 55 页

Hosting service, and at first, we used to get lots of questions and requests about the product. But around mid-2008, we began to notice a trend in the sort of requests we were getting:

但大约在 2008 年年中，我们开始注意到所收到请求中出现了一种趋势：

"Can you please give Subversion on Google Code the ability to hide
   specific branches?"

"Can you make it possible to create open source projects that start out
   hidden to the world and then are revealed when they’re ready?"

"Hi, I want to rewrite all my code from scratch, can you please wipe all
   the history?"

Can you spot a common theme to these requests? The answer is insecurity. People are afraid of others seeing and judging their work in progress. In one sense, insecurity is just a part of human nature—nobody likes to be criticized, especially for things that aren’t finished. Recognizing this theme tipped us off to a more general trend within software development: insecurity is actually a symptom of a larger problem.

你能看出这些请求的共同主题吗？答案是不安全感。人们害怕别人看到并评判自己尚未完成的工作。从某种意义上说，不安全感只是人性的一部分——没人喜欢被批评，尤其是为那些还没做完的东西被批评。识别出这个主题，让我们察觉到软件开发中一个更普遍的趋势：不安全感实际上是一个更大问题的症状。

The Genius Myth · 天才迷思

Many humans have the instinct to find and worship idols. For software engineers, those might be Linus Torvalds, Guido Van Rossum, Bill Gates—all heroes who changed the world with heroic feats. Linus wrote Linux by himself, right?

许多人天生有寻找并崇拜偶像的本能。对软件工程师来说，这些偶像可能是 Linus Torvalds、Guido Van Rossum、Bill Gates——都是凭英雄事迹改变世界的英雄。Linux 是 Linus 一个人写出来的，对吧？

Actually, what Linus did was write just the beginnings of a proof-of-concept Unix-like kernel and show it to an email list. That was no small accomplishment, and it was definitely an impressive achievement, but it was just the tip of the iceberg. Linux is hundreds of times bigger than that initial kernel and was developed by thousands of smart people. Linus’ real achievement was to lead these people and coordinate their work; Linux is the shining result not of his original idea, but of the collective labor of the community. (And Unix itself was not entirely written by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie, but by a group of smart people at Bell Labs.)

实际上，Linus 所做的，只是写出了一个概念验证的类 Unix 内核的雏形，并把它展示给一个邮件列表。这绝非小事，也确实是令人印象深刻的成就，但它只是冰山一角。Linux 比那个最初的内核大了几百倍，是由成千上万聪明人开发出来的。Linus 真正的成就，是领导这些人、协调他们的工作；Linux 这一辉煌成果，并非源于他最初的点子，而是社区集体劳动的结晶。（而且 Unix 本身也并非完全由 Ken Thompson 和 Dennis Ritchie 写成，而是贝尔实验室一群聪明人的成果。）

On that same note, did Guido Van Rossum personally write all of Python? Certainly, he wrote the first version. But hundreds of others were responsible for contributing to subsequent versions, including ideas, features, and bug fixes. Steve Jobs led an entire team that built the Macintosh, and although Bill Gates is known for writing a BASIC interpreter for early home computers, his bigger achievement was building a successful company around MS-DOS. Yet they all became leaders and symbols of the collective achievements of their communities. The Genius Myth is the tendency that we as humans need to ascribe the success of a team to a single person/leader.

同样，Guido Van Rossum 是亲手写完了整个 Python 吗？当然，他写了第一个版本。但后续版本是由成百上千人贡献的，包括想法、特性与缺陷修复。Steve Jobs 领导着一整支团队打造了 Macintosh；尽管 Bill Gates 以早期家用电脑的 BASIC 解释器闻名，他更大的成就是围绕 MS-DOS 建起了一家成功的公司。然而他们都成了各自社区集体成就的领导者与象征。天才迷思，就是我们人类倾向于把一个团队的成功归功于某一个人/领导者。

And what about Michael Jordan? It’s the same story. We idolized him, but the fact is that he didn’t win every basketball game by himself. His true genius was in the way he worked with his team. The team’s coach, Phil Jackson, was extremely clever, and his coaching techniques are legendary.

那 Michael Jordan 呢？同样的故事。我们把他偶像化，但事实是他并不是独自赢下每一场篮球赛的。他真正的天才在于他与团队协作的方式。球队教练 Phil Jackson 极其聪明，他的执教手法堪称传奇。

原书第 56 页

He recognized that one player alone never wins a championship, and so he assembled an entire “dream team” around MJ. This team was a well-oiled machine—at least as impressive as Michael himself.

他认识到单凭一个球员永远赢不了总冠军，于是围绕 MJ 组建了一整支“梦之队”。这支球队是一台运转良好的机器——至少和 Michael 本人一样令人印象深刻。

So, why do we repeatedly idolize the individual in these stories? Why do people buy products endorsed by celebrities? Why do we want to buy Michelle Obama’s dress or Michael Jordan’s shoes?

那么，我们为什么一再把这些故事里的个人偶像化？人们为什么买名人代言的产品？我们为什么想买 Michelle Obama 的那条裙子、或 Michael Jordan 的那双鞋？

Celebrity is a big part of it. Humans have a natural instinct to find leaders and role models, idolize them, and attempt to imitate them. We all need heroes for inspiration, and the programming world has its heroes, too. The phenomenon of “techie-celebrity” has almost spilled over into mythology. We all want to write something world-changing like Linux or design the next brilliant programming language.

名人效应是其中很大一部分。人类天生有寻找领导者与榜样、把他们偶像化并试图模仿的本能。我们都需要英雄来激励自己，编程界也有它的英雄。“技术名人”这一现象几乎已演变成神话。我们都想写出像 Linux 那样改变世界的东西，或设计出下一门出色的编程语言。

Deep down, many engineers secretly wish to be seen as geniuses. This fantasy goes something like this:

在内心深处，许多工程师都暗暗希望被看作天才。这种幻想大致是这样的：

  • You are struck by an awesome new concept.

    你被一个绝妙的新概念击中。

  • You vanish into your cave for weeks or months, slaving away at a perfect implementation of your idea.

    你消失进自己的洞穴里，花几周或几个月埋头苦干，把你的想法实现得尽善尽美。

  • You then “unleash” your software on the world, shocking everyone with your genius.

    然后你把软件“释放”给世界，用你的天才震惊所有人。

  • Your peers are astonished by your cleverness.

    你的同行被你的聪明惊得目瞪口呆。

  • People line up to use your software.

    人们排着队使用你的软件。

  • Fame and fortune follow naturally.

    名声与财富随之而来。

But hold on: time for a reality check. You’re probably not a genius. No offense, of course—we’re sure that you’re a very intelligent person. But do you realize how rare actual geniuses really are? Sure, you write code, and that’s a tricky skill. But even if you are a genius, it turns out that that’s not enough. Geniuses still make mistakes, and having brilliant ideas and elite programming skills doesn’t guarantee that your software will be a hit. Worse, you might find yourself solving only analytical problems and not human problems. Being a genius is most definitely not an excuse for being a jerk: anyone—genius or not—with poor social skills tends to be a poor teammate. The vast majority of the work at Google (and at most companies!) doesn’t require genius-level intellect, but 100% of the work requires a minimal level of social skills. What will make or break your career, especially at a company like Google, is how well you collaborate with others.

但且慢：该来一次现实检验了。你大概并不是天才。当然无意冒犯——我们确信你是个非常聪明的人。但你有没有意识到，真正的天才其实有多稀少？不错，你会写代码，这是一门棘手的技能。但即便你是天才，事实证明这也还不够。天才照样会犯错，拥有绝妙点子和顶尖编程技巧，并不能保证你的软件会大受欢迎。更糟的是，你可能发现自己只在解决分析性问题，而没有解决人的问题。是天才绝不能成为你当混蛋的借口：任何人——无论是不是天才——社交技巧差，往往都是个差劲的队友。Google（以及大多数公司！）里的绝大多数工作并不需要天才级的智力，但 100% 的工作都需要最低限度的社交技巧。决定你职业生涯成败的——尤其是在 Google 这样的公司——正是你与他人协作得有多好。

It turns out that this Genius Myth is just another manifestation of our insecurity. Many programmers are afraid to share work they’ve only just started because it means peers will see their mistakes and know the author of the code is not a genius.

事实证明，这种天才迷思只是我们不安全感的又一种表现。许多程序员害怕分享自己刚刚起步的工作，因为那意味着同行会看到他们的错误，并知道这段代码的作者并不是天才。

原书第 57 页

To quote a friend:

引用一位朋友的话：

I know I get SERIOUSLY insecure about people looking before something
is done. Like they are going to seriously judge me and think I’m an idiot.

This is an extremely common feeling among programmers, and the natural reaction is to hide in a cave, work, work, work, and then polish, polish, polish, sure that no one will see your goof-ups and that you’ll still have a chance to unveil your masterpiece when you’re done. Hide away until your code is perfect.

这种感受在程序员中极为普遍，而自然反应就是躲进洞穴，工作、工作、再工作，然后打磨、打磨、再打磨，确信没人会看到你的糗事，并且等你做完后还有机会揭开你的杰作。把自己藏起来，直到代码完美无缺。

Another common motivation for hiding your work is the fear that another programmer might take your idea and run with it before you get around to working on it. By keeping it secret, you control the idea. We know what you’re probably thinking now: so what? Shouldn’t people be allowed to work however they want? Actually, no. In this case, we assert that you’re doing it wrong, and it is a big deal. Here’s why.

藏起工作的另一个常见动机，是害怕另一个程序员在你还没动手之前就把你的点子拿走、抢先实现。通过保密，你就掌控了这个点子。我们知道你现在大概在想：那又怎样？难道不该允许人们按自己喜欢的方式工作吗？实际上，不行。在这件事上，我们断言你做错了，而且这很要紧。原因如下。

Hiding Considered Harmful · 隐藏被认为有害

If you spend all of your time working alone, you’re increasing the risk of unnecessary failure and cheating your potential for growth. Even though software development is deeply intellectual work that can require deep concentration and alone time, you must play that off against the value (and need!) for collaboration and review. First of all, how do you even know whether you’re on the right track?

如果你把所有时间都花在独自工作上，你就是在增加不必要失败的风险，也在辜负自己成长的潜力。尽管软件开发是高度智力的工作、可能需要深度专注和独处时间，你也必须把它与协作和评审的价值（以及必要性！）权衡。首先，你怎么知道自己走的路对不对？

Imagine you’re a bicycle-design enthusiast, and one day you get a brilliant idea for a completely new way to design a gear shifter. You order parts and proceed to spend weeks holed up in your garage trying to build a prototype. When your neighbor—also a bike enthusiast—asks you what’s up, you decide not to talk about it. You don’t want anyone to know about your project until it’s absolutely perfect. Another few months go by and you’re having trouble making your prototype work correctly. But because you’re working in secrecy, it’s impossible to solicit advice from your mechanically inclined friends.

想象你是一个自行车设计爱好者，有一天你冒出一个绝妙的点子：用一种全新方式设计一个拨链器。你订了零件，然后钻进车库里花了几周试图造一个原型。当你的邻居——同样是自行车爱好者——问你在忙什么时，你决定不说。你不想让任何人知道你的项目，直到它绝对完美。又过了几个月，你在让原型正常工作上遇到了麻烦。但因为你是秘密进行的，根本没法向那些懂机械的朋友征求建议。

Then, one day your neighbor pulls his bike out of his garage with a radical new gear-shifting mechanism. Turns out he’s been building something very similar to your invention, but with the help of some friends down at the bike shop. At this point, you’re exasperated. You show him your work. He points out that your design had some simple flaws—ones that might have been fixed in the first week if you had shown him. There are a number of lessons to learn here.

然后，有一天，你的邻居从车库里推出他的自行车，上面装着一个激进的新变速机构。原来他一直在造一个和你的发明非常相似的东西，只不过是在车店里几个朋友的帮助下做的。这时你气急败坏。你把自己的作品给他看。他指出你的设计有一些简单的缺陷——要是你第一周就给他看，那些缺陷当时就能修掉。这里有好几个教训可汲取。

原书第 58 页

Early Detection · 及早发现

If you keep your great idea hidden from the world and refuse to show anyone anything until the implementation is polished, you’re taking a huge gamble. It’s easy to make fundamental design mistakes early on. You risk reinventing wheels. And you forfeit the benefits of collaboration, too: notice how much faster your neighbor moved by working with others? This is why people dip their toes in the water before jumping in the deep end: you need to make sure that you’re working on the right thing, you’re doing it correctly, and it hasn’t been done before. The chances of an early misstep are high. The more feedback you solicit early on, the more you lower this risk. Remember the tried-and-true mantra of “Fail early, fail fast, fail often.”

如果你把自己的好点子对世界藏起来、拒绝在实现打磨好之前给任何人看任何东西，你就是在下一场巨大的赌注。在早期很容易犯根本性的设计错误。你有重复造轮子的风险。你也放弃了协作的好处：注意到你的邻居因为和别人合作而推进得快多了吗？这就是为什么人们在跳进深水区之前先试探水温：你需要确认自己在做正确的事、做法正确、而且以前没人做过。早期走错步的概率很高。你越早征求反馈，就越能降低这个风险。记住那句久经考验的箴言：“早失败、快失败、常失败。”

Early sharing isn’t just about preventing personal missteps and getting your ideas vetted. It’s also important to strengthen what we call the bus factor of your project.

及早分享，不仅仅是为了防止个人走错步、让你的点子被审查。它对增强我们所谓项目的“巴士因子（bus factor）”也很重要。

The Bus Factor · 巴士因子

Bus factor (noun): the number of people that need to get hit by a bus
before your project is completely doomed.

How dispersed is the knowledge and know-how in your project? If you’re the only person who understands how the prototype code works, you might enjoy good job security—but if you get hit by a bus, the project is toast. If you’re working with a colleague, however, you’ve doubled the bus factor. And if you have a small team designing and prototyping together, things are even better—the project won’t be marooned when a team member disappears. Remember: team members might not literally be hit by buses, but other unpredictable life events still happen. Someone might get married, move away, leave the company, or take leave to care for a sick relative. Ensuring that there is at least good documentation in addition to a primary and a secondary owner for each area of responsibility helps future-proof your project’s success and increases your project’s bus factor. Hopefully most engineers recognize that it is better to be one part of a successful project than the critical part of a failed project.

你的项目里的知识与技术诀窍分布得有多散？如果你是唯一理解原型代码如何工作的人，你也许能享有不错的工作保障——但如果你被公交车撞了，项目就完蛋了。然而如果你和一位同事一起工作，你就把巴士因子翻了一倍。而如果你们有一个小团队一起设计和做原型，那就更好——当一名团队成员消失时，项目不会被搁浅。记住：团队成员未必真的被公交车撞，但其他不可预测的人生事件照样会发生。有人可能结婚、搬走、离职，或请假去照顾生病的亲属。为每个责任领域除了一名主负责人和一名副负责人之外，再确保有良好的文档，这有助于让项目的成功经得起未来考验，也提高了项目的巴士因子。但愿大多数工程师都认识到：做一个成功项目的一部分，胜过做一个失败项目的关键部分。

Beyond the bus factor, there’s the issue of overall pace of progress. It’s easy to forget that working alone is often a tough slog, much slower than people want to admit. How much do you learn when working alone? How fast do you move? Google and Stack Overflow are great sources of opinions and information, but they’re no substitute for actual human experience. Working with other people directly increases the collective wisdom behind the effort. When you become stuck on something absurd, how much time do you waste pulling yourself out of the hole? Think about how

除了巴士因子，还有整体推进速度的问题。人们很容易忘记：独自工作往往是一场艰难的跋涉，比人们愿意承认的慢得多。独自工作时你能学到多少？你能推进多快？Google 和 Stack Overflow 是观点与信息的绝佳来源，但它们无法替代真实的人的经验。直接与他人共事，能增加这项努力背后的集体智慧。当你卡在某个荒谬的问题上时，你要浪费多少时间才能把自己从坑里爬出来？想想看，如果有几个同伴在你肩头看一眼、立刻告诉你哪里搞错了、该怎么越过这个问题，体验会多么不同。

原书第 59 页

different the experience would be if you had a couple of peers to look over your shoulder and tell you—instantly—how you goofed and how to get past the problem. This is exactly why teams sit together (or do pair programming) in software engineering companies. Programming is hard. Software engineering is even harder. You need that second pair of eyes.

这正是为什么在软件工程公司里，团队要坐在一起（或结对编程）。编程很难，软件工程更难。你需要那第二双眼睛。

Pace of Progress · 推进的节奏

Here’s another analogy. Think about how you work with your compiler. When you sit down to write a large piece of software, do you spend days writing 10,000 lines of code, and then, after writing that final, perfect line, press the “compile” button for the very first time? Of course you don’t. Can you imagine what sort of disaster would result? Programmers work best in tight feedback loops: write a new function, compile. Add a test, compile. Refactor some code, compile. This way, we discover and fix typos and bugs as soon as possible after generating code. We want the compiler at our side for every little step; some environments can even compile our code as we type. This is how we keep code quality high and make sure our software is evolving correctly, bit by bit. The current DevOps philosophy toward tech productivity is explicit about these sorts of goals: get feedback as early as possible, test as early as possible, and think about security and production environments as early as possible. This is all bundled into the idea of “shifting left” in the developer workflow; the earlier we find a problem, the cheaper it is to fix it.

再打个比方。想想你是怎么和编译器打交道的。当你坐下来写一大块软件时，你会花好几天写 10000 行代码，然后在写完最后那行完美代码之后，才第一次按下“编译”键吗？你当然不会。你能想象那会酿成什么样的灾难吗？程序员在紧密的反馈循环里工作得最好：写一个新函数，编译。加一个测试，编译。重构一些代码，编译。这样，我们在生成代码后尽快发现并修复笔误和 bug。我们希望编译器在每一小步都陪在身边；有些环境甚至能在我们键入时就编译。这就是我们保持代码质量高、确保软件一点一点正确演进的方式。当今 DevOps 对技术生产力的哲学，对这类目标说得很明白：尽早获得反馈、尽早测试、尽早考虑安全与生产环境。这一切都被打包进开发者工作流中“左移”的理念里；我们越早发现问题，修复它就越便宜。

The same sort of rapid feedback loop is needed not just at the code level, but at the whole-project level, too. Ambitious projects evolve quickly and must adapt to changing environments as they go. Projects run into unpredictable design obstacles or political hazards, or we simply discover that things aren’t working as planned. Requirements morph unexpectedly. How do you get that feedback loop so that you know the instant your plans or designs need to change? Answer: by working in a team. Most engineers know the quote, “Many eyes make all bugs shallow,” but a better version might be, “Many eyes make sure your project stays relevant and on track.” People working in caves awaken to discover that while their original vision might be complete, the world has changed and their project has become irrelevant.

同样这种快速反馈循环，不仅在代码层面需要，在整个项目层面也需要。有雄心的项目演进很快，必须在行进中适应不断变化的环境。项目会撞上不可预测的设计障碍或政治风险，或者我们只是发现事情并没有按计划进行。需求会意外地变形。你如何才能拥有那个反馈循环，让你在计划或设计需要改变的那一刻就知道？答案是：在团队中工作。大多数工程师都知道那句话：“多双眼睛让所有 bug 都变浅。”但一个更好的版本也许是：“多双眼睛确保你的项目始终切题、不跑偏。”在洞穴里工作的人醒来后会发现：虽然自己当初的愿景也许完成了，但世界已经变了，他们的项目已经变得无关紧要。

Case Study: Engineers and Offices · 案例：工程师与办公室

Twenty-five years ago, conventional wisdom stated that for an engineer to be productive, they needed to have their own office with a door that closed. This was supposedly the only way they could have big, uninterrupted slabs of time to deeply concentrate on writing reams of code.

25 年前，传统观念认为：工程师要想高产，就需要有一间带门、能关上门的私人办公室。据说这是他们能拥有大块、不被打断的时间、从而深度专注于写大量代码的唯一方式。

原书第 60 页

I think that it’s not only unnecessary for most engineers to be in a private office, it’s downright dangerous. Software today is written by teams, not individuals, and a high-bandwidth, readily available connection to the rest of your team is even more valuable than your internet connection. You can have all the uninterrupted time in the world, but if you’re using it to work on the wrong thing, you’re wasting your time. Unfortunately, it seems that modern-day tech companies (including Google, in some cases) have swung the pendulum to the exact opposite extreme. Walk into their offices and you’ll often find engineers clustered together in massive rooms—a hundred or more people together—with no walls whatsoever. This “open floor plan” is now a topic of huge debate and, as a result, hostility toward open offices is on the rise. The tiniest conversation becomes public, and people end up not talking for risk of annoying dozens of neighbors. This is just as bad as private offices! We think the middle ground is really the best solution. Group teams of four to eight people together in small rooms (or large offices) to make it easy (and non-embarrassing) for spontaneous conversation to happen.

我认为，对大多数工程师来说，待在私人办公室里不仅没有必要，而且简直是危险的。今天的软件是由团队、而不是个人写的；与团队其他成员之间一条高带宽、随叫随到的连接，甚至比你的互联网连接更有价值。你可以拥有世上所有不被打扰的时间，但如果你用它在做错误的事，你就是在浪费时间。不幸的是，如今的科技公司（包括某些情况下的 Google）似乎把钟摆摆到了完全相反的极端。走进它们的办公室，你常会发现工程师们挤在巨大的房间里——一百多人共处一室——毫无隔断。这种“开放式平面布局”如今成了巨大争议的话题，结果人们对开放式办公室的敌意也在上升。最微小的交谈都变成了公开的，人们最终因为怕惹恼几十个邻居而干脆不说话。这和私人办公室一样糟糕！我们认为中间路线才是真正最好的解法。把四到八人的小组安排在小房间（或大办公室）里，让自发的交谈能够轻易（且不尴尬地）发生。

Of course, in any situation, individual engineers still need a way to filter out noise and interruptions, which is why most teams I’ve seen have developed a way to communicate that they’re currently busy and that you should limit interruptions. Some of us used to work on a team with a vocal interrupt protocol: if you wanted to talk, you would say “Breakpoint Mary,” where Mary was the name of the person you wanted to talk to. If Mary was at a point where she could stop, she would swing her chair around and listen. If Mary was too busy, she’d just say “ack,” and you’d go on with other things until she finished with her current head state. Other teams have tokens or stuffed animals that team members put on their monitor to signify that they should be interrupted only in case of emergency. Still other teams give out noise-canceling headphones to engineers to make it easier to deal with background noise—in fact, in many companies, the very act of wearing headphones is a common signal that means “don’t disturb me unless it’s really important.” Many engineers tend to go into headphones-only mode when coding, which may be useful for short spurts but, if used all the time, can be just as bad for collaboration as walling yourself off in an office.

当然，在任何情况下，单个工程师仍然需要一种过滤噪音与打扰的方式，这就是为什么我见过的大多数团队都发展出了一种沟通方式，表明自己现在很忙、你应该减少打扰。我们有些人曾在一个团队里用过一套口头打断协议：如果你想说话，就喊“Breakpoint Mary”，Mary 是你想找的那个人的名字。如果 Mary 正处在可以停下的点上，她就会转过椅子来听；如果 Mary 太忙，她就回一句“ack”，你就去忙别的，直到她结束当前的思维状态。另一些团队用令牌或毛绒玩具，放在显示器上，表示只有紧急情况才能打断。还有一些团队给工程师发降噪耳机，让他们更容易应对背景噪音——事实上，在许多公司，戴耳机这个动作本身就是一个常见信号，意思是“除非真的重要，否则别打扰我”。许多工程师在写代码时倾向进入“只戴耳机”模式，这对短时间冲刺也许有用，但如果一直用，对协作的危害可能和把自己隔在办公室里一样糟。

Don’t misunderstand us—we still think engineers need uninterrupted time to focus on writing code, but we think they need a high-bandwidth, low-friction connection to their team just as much. If less-knowledgeable people on your team feel that there’s a barrier to asking you a question, it’s a problem: finding the right balance is an art.

别误会我们——我们仍然认为工程师需要不被打扰的时间来专注写代码，但我们同样认为他们需要与团队之间一条高带宽、低摩擦的连接。如果你团队里那些知识较少的人觉得向你提问存在障碍，那就是个问题：找到恰当的平衡是一门艺术。

原书第 61 页

In Short, Don’t Hide · 简而言之，别藏

So, what “hiding” boils down to is this: working alone is inherently riskier than working with others. Even though you might be afraid of someone stealing your idea or thinking you’re not intelligent, you should be much more concerned about wasting huge swaths of your time toiling away on the wrong thing. Don’t become another statistic.

那么，“隐藏”归结起来就是：独自工作本质上比与他人共事风险更高。尽管你也许害怕有人偷走你的点子、或觉得你不聪明，但你更应该担心的是：把大段大段时间浪费在错误的事情上。别成为又一个统计数字。

It’s All About the Team · 一切都关乎团队

So, let’s back up now and put all of these ideas together. The point we’ve been hammering away at is that, in the realm of programming, lone craftspeople are extremely rare—and even when they do exist, they don’t perform superhuman achievements in a vacuum; their world-changing accomplishment is almost always the result of a spark of inspiration followed by a heroic team effort. A great team makes brilliant use of its superstars, but the whole is always greater than the sum of its parts. But creating a superstar team is fiendishly difficult. Let’s put this idea into simpler words: software engineering is a team endeavor.

那么，现在让我们退一步，把这些想法拼到一起。我们一直在反复强调的是：在编程领域，孤独的手艺人极其稀少——即便他们真的存在，也不会在真空中做出超人般的成就；他们那改变世界的成果，几乎总是一闪灵感火花之后、一番英雄般团队努力的结果。一支伟大的团队会出色地利用它的明星成员，但整体总是大于部分之和。然而打造一支明星团队难如登天。让我们用更简单的话来说：软件工程是一项团队事业。

This concept directly contradicts the inner Genius Programmer fantasy so many of us hold, but it’s not enough to be brilliant when you’re alone in your hacker’s lair. You’re not going to change the world or delight millions of computer users by hiding and preparing your secret invention. You need to work with other people. Share your vision. Divide the labor. Learn from others. Create a brilliant team. Consider this: how many pieces of widely used, successful software can you name that were truly written by a single person? (Some people might say “LaTeX,” but it’s hardly “widely used,” unless you consider the number of people writing scientific papers to be a statistically significant portion of all computer users!) High-functioning teams are gold and the true key to success. You should be aiming for this experience however you can.

这个概念与我们许多人内心那个“天才程序员”的幻想直接相悖：独自待在黑客巢穴里再聪明也不够。你不可能靠躲起来准备你的秘密发明来改变世界、取悦数百万电脑用户。你需要和别人一起工作。分享你的愿景，分工，向他人学习，打造一支出色的团队。想想看：你能说出多少个被广泛使用、获得成功、却真正由一个人写成的软件？（有些人可能会说“LaTeX”，但它很难算“被广泛使用”——除非你认为写科学论文的人在所有电脑用户中占统计上显著的比例！）高效运转的团队是黄金，是成功的真正钥匙。你应当尽一切可能去追求这种体验。

The Three Pillars of Social Interaction · 社交互动的三大支柱

So, if teamwork is the best route to producing great software, how does one build (or find) a great team? To reach collaborative nirvana, you first need to learn and embrace what I call the “three pillars” of social skills. These three principles aren’t just about greasing the wheels of relationships; they’re the foundation on which all healthy interaction and collaboration are based:

那么，如果团队协作是产出优秀软件的最佳途径，一个人该如何打造（或找到）一支伟大的团队？要达到协作的涅槃，你首先需要学习并拥抱我所说的社交技能“三大支柱”。这三条原则不只是给关系润滑；它们是一切健康互动与协作所赖以建立的根基：

原书第 62 页

  • Pillar 1: Humility. You are not the center of the universe (nor is your code!). You’re neither omniscient nor infallible. You’re open to self-improvement.

    支柱一：谦逊。你不是宇宙的中心（你的代码也不是！）。你既非全知，也非绝不犯错。你对自我提升持开放态度。

  • Pillar 2: Respect. You genuinely care about others you work with. You treat them kindly and appreciate their abilities and accomplishments.

    支柱二：尊重。你真心关心与你共事的人。你善待他们，欣赏他们的能力与成就。

  • Pillar 3: Trust. You believe others are competent and will do the right thing, and you’re OK with letting them drive when appropriate.

    支柱三：信任。你相信他人有能力、会做正确的事，并且在合适的时候乐于让他们掌舵。

If you perform a root-cause analysis on almost any social conflict, you can ultimately trace it back to a lack of humility, respect, and/or trust. That might sound implausible at first, but give it a try. Think about some nasty or uncomfortable social situation currently in your life. At the basest level, is everyone being appropriately humble? Are people really respecting one another? Is there mutual trust?

如果你对几乎任何一场社交冲突做一次根因分析，最终都能把它追溯到谦逊、尊重和/或信任的缺失。这起初听起来也许难以置信，但试一试。想想你生活中某件令人不快或尴尬的社交情境。在最基础的层面上，每个人都表现得足够谦逊吗？人们真的在互相尊重吗？存在相互信任吗？

Why Do These Pillars Matter? · 这些支柱为什么重要？

When you began this chapter, you probably weren’t planning to sign up for some sort of weekly support group. We empathize. Dealing with social problems can be difficult: people are messy, unpredictable, and often annoying to interface with. Rather than putting energy into analyzing social situations and making strategic moves, it’s tempting to write off the whole effort. It’s much easier to hang out with a predictable compiler, isn’t it? Why bother with the social stuff at all?

当你开始读这一章时，你大概没打算报名参加某种每周互助小组。我们理解。处理社交问题可能很困难：人是混乱的、不可预测的，打交道时常常令人恼火。与其把精力花在分析社交情境和做战略性动作上，不如干脆放弃这一切——这很诱人。和一个可预测的编译器待在一起要轻松得多，不是吗？何必费劲搞这些社交的东西？

Here’s a quote from a famous lecture by Richard Hamming:

下面是 Richard Hamming 那场著名演讲中的一段话：

By taking the trouble to tell jokes to the secretaries and being a little
friendly, I got superb secretarial help. For instance, one time for some
idiot reason all the reproducing services at Murray Hill were tied up. Don’t
ask me how, but they were. I wanted something done. My secretary called up
somebody at Holmdel, hopped [into] the company car, made the hour-long trip
down and got it reproduced, and then came back. It was a payoff for the
times I had made an effort to cheer her up, tell her jokes and be friendly;
it was that little extra work that later paid off for me. By realizing you
have to use the system and studying how to get the system to do your work,
you learn how to adapt the system to your desires.

The moral is this: do not underestimate the power of playing the social game. It’s not about tricking or manipulating people; it’s about creating relationships to get things done. Relationships always outlast projects. When you’ve got richer relationships with your coworkers, they’ll be more willing to go the extra mile when you need them.

寓意在于：不要低估“玩社交游戏”的力量。这不是要欺骗或操纵别人；而是建立关系以把事情做成。关系总是比项目更长久。当你与同事拥有更丰厚的关系时，在你需要他们的时候，他们会更愿意多走那一英里。

原书第 63 页

Humility, Respect, and Trust in Practice · 谦逊、尊重与信任的实践

All of this preaching about humility, respect, and trust sounds like a sermon. Let’s come out of the clouds and think about how to apply these ideas in real-life situations. We’re going to examine a list of specific behaviors and examples that you can start with. Many of them might sound obvious at first, but after you begin thinking about them, you’ll notice how often you (and your peers) are guilty of not following them—we’ve certainly noticed this about ourselves!

所有这些关于谦逊、尊重与信任的说教听起来像一通布道。让我们走出云端，想想如何在现实情境中应用这些理念。我们要审视一份具体行为与示例的清单，供你起步。其中许多起初听起来显而易见，但当你开始思考它们时，就会注意到你（和你的同行）有多少次在违背它们——我们自己当然也注意到了这一点！

Lose the ego. OK, this is sort of a simpler way of telling someone without enough humility to lose their ’tude. Nobody wants to work with someone who consistently behaves like they’re the most important person in the room. Even if you know you’re the wisest person in the discussion, don’t wave it in people’s faces. For example, do you always feel like you need to have the first or last word on every subject? Do you feel the need to comment on every detail in a proposal or discussion? Or do you know somebody who does these things? Although it’s important to be humble, that doesn’t mean you need to be a doormat; there’s nothing wrong with self-confidence. Just don’t come off like a know-it-all. Even better, think about going for a “collective” ego, instead; rather than worrying about whether you’re personally awesome, try to build a sense of team accomplishment and group pride. For example, the Apache Software Foundation has a long history of creating communities around software projects. These communities have incredibly strong identities and reject people who are more concerned with self-promotion.

放下自我（Lose the ego）。好吧，这算是一种更简单的说法，告诉那些不够谦逊的人收起自己的态度。没人愿意和一个总表现得自己是屋里最重要人物的人共事。即便你知道自己是讨论中最有智慧的人，也别把它甩到别人脸上。例如，你是否总觉得每个话题都得自己第一个或最后一个发言？你是否觉得对一个提案或讨论的每个细节都要评论一番？或者你认识某个这样做的人？虽然谦逊很重要，但那并不意味着你得当受气包；自信并没有错。只是别表现得像个万事通。更进一步，试着追求一种“集体”的自我；与其担心你个人是否牛，不如努力建立团队成就感与集体自豪感。例如，Apache 软件基金会在围绕软件项目创建社区方面有着悠久历史。这些社区有着极强的认同感，会排斥那些更在乎自我推销的人。

Ego manifests itself in many ways, and a lot of the time, it can get in the way of your productivity and slow you down. Here’s another great story from Hamming’s lecture that illustrates this point perfectly (emphasis ours):

自我以多种方式显现，而且很多时候它会妨碍你的生产力、拖慢你的脚步。下面是 Hamming 演讲中又一个完美说明这一点的精彩故事（着重为我们所加）：

John Tukey almost always dressed very casually. He would go into an
important office and it would take a long time before the other fellow
realized that this is a first-class man and he had better listen. For a long
time, John has had to overcome this kind of hostility. It’s wasted effort! I
didn’t say you should conform; I said, "The appearance of conforming gets you
a long way." If you chose to assert your ego in any number of ways, "I am
going to do it my way," you pay a small steady price throughout the whole of
your professional career. And this, over a whole lifetime, adds up to an
enormous amount of needless trouble. […] By realizing you have to use the
system and studying how to get the system to do your work, you learn how to
adapt the system to your desires. Or you can fight it steadily, as a small,
undeclared war, for the whole of your life.
原书第 64 页

Learn to give and take criticism. A few years ago, Joe started a new job as a programmer. After his first week, he really began digging into the codebase. Because he cared about what was going on, he started gently questioning other teammates about their contributions. He sent simple code reviews by email, politely asking about design assumptions or pointing out places where logic could be improved. After a couple of weeks, he was summoned to his director’s office. “What’s the problem?” Joe asked. “Did I do something wrong?” The director looked concerned: “We’ve had a lot of complaints about your behavior, Joe. Apparently, you’ve been really harsh toward your teammates, criticizing them left and right. They’re upset. You need to tone it down.” Joe was utterly baffled. Surely, he thought, his code reviews should have been welcomed and appreciated by his peers.

学会给出和接受批评。几年前，Joe 开始了一份程序员的新工作。第一周之后，他真正开始钻研代码库。因为他关心正在发生的事，他开始温和地向其他队友询问他们的贡献。他通过邮件发出简单的代码评审，礼貌地询问设计假设，或指出逻辑可以改进的地方。几周后，他被叫到总监办公室。“怎么了？”Joe 问，“我做错什么了吗？”总监面露忧色：“我们收到很多关于你行为的投诉，Joe。显然你对队友非常苛刻，到处批评他们。他们很难过。你得收敛一点。”Joe 完全懵了。他心想，自己的代码评审理应受到同行欢迎和赞赏才对。

In this case, however, Joe should have been more sensitive to the team’s widespread insecurity and should have used a subtler means to introduce code reviews into the culture—perhaps even something as simple as discussing the idea with the team in advance and asking team members to try it out for a few weeks. In a professional software engineering environment, criticism is almost never personal—it’s usually just part of the process of making a better project. The trick is to make sure you (and those around you) understand the difference between a constructive criticism of someone’s creative output and a flat-out assault against someone’s character. The latter is useless—it’s petty and nearly impossible to act on. The former can (and should!) be helpful and give guidance on how to improve. And, most important, it’s imbued with respect: the person giving the constructive criticism genuinely cares about the other person and wants them to improve themselves or their work. Learn to respect your peers and give constructive criticism politely. If you truly respect someone, you’ll be motivated to choose tactful, helpful phrasing—a skill acquired with much practice. We cover this much more in Chapter 9.

然而在这件事上，Joe 本应对团队普遍的不安全感更敏感，也本应采用一种更微妙的方式把代码评审引入文化——哪怕只是提前和团队讨论这个想法、请大家试用几周，也行。在专业的软件工程环境里，批评几乎从来不是针对个人的——它通常只是把项目做得更好这一过程的一部分。诀窍在于确保你（以及你身边的人）分清：对某人创造性产出的建设性批评，与对某人人格的直接攻击，是两回事。后者毫无用处——它小气，而且几乎无法据此采取行动。前者则能够（也应该！）有帮助、给出如何改进的指引。而且最重要的是，它饱含尊重：给出建设性批评的人真心关心对方，希望对方改进自己或自己的工作。学会尊重你的同行，礼貌地给出建设性批评。如果你真的尊重某个人，你就会有动力去选择得体、有益的措辞——这是一种需要大量练习才能获得的技能。我们在第 9 章对此讨论得更多。

On the other side of the conversation, you need to learn to accept criticism as well. This means not just being humble about your skills, but trusting that the other person has your best interests (and those of your project!) at heart and doesn’t actually think you’re an idiot. Programming is a skill like anything else: it improves with practice. If a peer pointed out ways in which you could improve your juggling, would you take it as an attack on your character and value as a human being? We hope not. In the same way, your self-worth shouldn’t be connected to the code you write—or any creative project you build. To repeat ourselves: you are not your code. Say that over and over. You are not what you make. You need to not only believe it yourself, but get your coworkers to believe it, too.

在对话的另一端，你还需要学会接受批评。这不仅意味着对自己的技能保持谦逊，还意味着相信对方心里是为你（和你的项目！）好，并不是真的觉得你是个白痴。编程和其他任何技能一样：靠练习提高。如果一个同行指出你在杂耍上可以改进的地方，你会把它当作对你人格与做人价值的攻击吗？我们希望不会。同样，你的自我价值不应该与你写的代码——或你构建的任何创造性项目——挂钩。我们再说一遍：你不是你的代码。把这句话反复念。你不是你所造之物。你不仅要自己相信，还要让你的同事也相信。

For example, if you have an insecure collaborator, here’s what not to say: “Man, you totally got the control flow wrong on that method there. You should be using the standard xyzzy code pattern like everyone else.” This feedback is full of antipatterns: you’re telling someone they’re “wrong” (as if the world were black and white), demanding they change something, and accusing them of creating something that

例如，如果你有一位缺乏安全感的合作者，下面这些话千万别说：“老兄，你那个方法的控制流完全写错了。你应该像其他人一样用标准的 xyzzy 代码模式。”这种反馈充满了反模式：你在说某人“错了”（好像世界是非黑即白的），要求他们改东西，还指责他们做的事与其他人做的相悖（让他们觉得自己蠢）。你的同事会立刻进入防御姿态，而他们的回应必然会过于情绪化。

原书第 65 页

goes against what everyone else is doing (making them feel stupid). Your coworker will immediately be put on the offense, and their response is bound to be overly emotional. A better way to say the same thing might be, “Hey, I’m confused by the control flow in this section here. I wonder if the xyzzy code pattern might make this clearer and easier to maintain?” Notice how you’re using humility to make the question about you, not them. They’re not wrong; you’re just having trouble understanding the code. The suggestion is merely offered up as a way to clarify things for poor little you while possibly helping the project’s long-term sustainability goals. You’re also not demanding anything—you’re giving your collaborator the ability to peacefully reject the suggestion. The discussion stays focused on the code itself, not on anyone’s value or coding skills.

同样的意思，一个更好的说法也许是：“嘿，我对这一段的控制流有点困惑。我在想用 xyzzy 代码模式是不是能让这里更清晰、更容易维护？”注意你是如何用谦逊把问题变成关于你自己、而不是关于他们的。他们没有错；只是你理解这段代码有点困难。这个建议仅仅是作为一种帮可怜的你把事情弄清楚的方式提出来，同时也许还能助力项目的长期可持续性目标。你也没有要求任何事——你给了合作者平静地拒绝这个建议的余地。讨论始终聚焦于代码本身，而不是任何人的价值或编程技巧。

Fail fast and iterate · 快速失败、迭代改进

There’s a well-known urban legend in the business world about a manager who makes a mistake and loses an impressive $10 million. He dejectedly goes into the office the next day and starts packing up his desk, and when he gets the inevitable “the CEO wants to see you in his office” call, he trudges into the CEO’s office and quietly slides a piece of paper across the desk.

商业界有一个广为人知的都市传说：一位经理犯了个错，亏了令人咋舌的 1000 万美元。第二天他沮丧地走进办公室，开始收拾办公桌；当那个不可避免的“CEO 要见你”的电话打来时，他步履沉重地走进 CEO 办公室，把一张纸轻轻滑过桌面。

"What’s this?" asks the CEO.
"My resignation," says the executive. "I assume you called me in here to
   fire me."
"Fire you?" responds the CEO, incredulously. "Why would I fire you? I just
   spent $10 million training you!"

It’s an extreme story, to be sure, but the CEO in this story understands that firing the executive wouldn’t undo the $10 million loss, and it would compound it by losing a valuable executive who he can be very sure won’t make that kind of mistake again. At Google, one of our favorite mottos is that “Failure is an option.” It’s widely recognized that if you’re not failing now and then, you’re not being innovative enough or taking enough risks. Failure is viewed as a golden opportunity to learn and improve for the next go-around. In fact, Thomas Edison is often quoted as saying, “If I find 10,000 ways something won’t work, I haven’t failed. I am not discouraged, because every wrong attempt discarded is another step forward.”

这当然是个极端的故事，但故事里的 CEO 明白：解雇这位高管并不能挽回那 1000 万美元的损失，反而会因为失去一位宝贵的高管而雪上加霜——他几乎可以肯定这位高管今后不会再犯这种错。在 Google，我们最喜欢的格言之一是：“失败是一种选项（Failure is an option）。”人们普遍认识到：如果你不偶尔失败一下，说明你的创新还不够、承担的风险还不够。失败被视为一次黄金机会，去学习、为下一轮改进。事实上，人们常引用 Thomas Edison 的话：“如果我找到了一万种行不通的方法，我并没有失败。我并不气馁，因为每排除一个错误的尝试，就是又向前迈了一步。”

Over in Google X—the division that works on “moonshots” like self-driving cars and internet access delivered by balloons—failure is deliberately built into its incentive system. People come up with outlandish ideas and coworkers are actively encouraged

在 Google X——那个致力于自动驾驶汽车、气球提供上网等“登月项目”的部门——失败被刻意地纳入了它的激励体系。人们提出各种异想天开的点子，而同事们被积极鼓励尽快把它们毙掉。

to shoot them down as fast as possible. Individuals are rewarded (and even compete) to see how many ideas they can disprove or invalidate in a fixed period of time. Only when a concept truly cannot be debunked at a whiteboard by all peers does it proceed to early prototype.

个人会因为在固定时间内能证伪或推翻多少个点子而获得奖励（甚至相互竞赛）。只有当一个概念在白板前真的被所有同行都无法驳倒时，它才会进入早期原型阶段。

Blameless Post-Mortem Culture · 不指责的事后复盘文化

The key to learning from your mistakes is to document your failures by performing a root-cause analysis and writing up a “postmortem,” as it’s called at Google (and many other companies). Take extra care to make sure the postmortem document isn’t just a useless list of apologies or excuses or finger-pointing—that’s not its purpose. A proper postmortem should always contain an explanation of what was learned and what is going to change as a result of the learning experience. Then, make sure that the postmortem is readily accessible and that the team really follows through on the proposed changes. Properly documenting failures also makes it easier for other people (present and future) to know what happened and avoid repeating history. Don’t erase your tracks—light them up like a runway for those who follow you!

从错误中学习的关键，是通过做根因分析、写下一份“事后复盘（postmortem）”（Google 及许多其他公司的叫法）来记录你的失败。要格外注意：复盘文档不该只是一堆没用的道歉、借口或指责——那不是它的目的。一份像样的复盘，应当总是包含对“学到了什么”以及“作为这次学习经历的结果，将做出什么改变”的说明。然后，确保这份复盘容易被找到，并且团队真的跟进落实所提出的变更。恰当地记录失败，也让其他人（现在的和未来的）更容易知道发生了什么、避免重蹈覆辙。别抹去你的痕迹——把它们像跑道一样点亮，留给后来者！

A good postmortem should include the following:

一份好的复盘应包含以下内容：

  • A brief summary of the event

    事件的简要总结

  • A timeline of the event, from discovery through investigation to resolution

    事件的时间线：从发现、调查到解决

  • The primary cause of the event

    事件的根本原因

  • Impact and damage assessment

    影响与损失评估

  • A set of action items (with owners) to fix the problem immediately

    一组立即修复问题的行动项（含负责人）

  • A set of action items to prevent the event from happening again

    一组防止事件再次发生的行动项

  • Lessons learned

    学到的教训

Learn patience · 学会耐心

Years ago, I was writing a tool to convert CVS repositories to Subversion (and later, Git). Due to the vagaries of CVS, I kept unearthing bizarre bugs. Because my long-time friend and coworker Karl knew CVS quite intimately, we decided we should work together to fix these bugs. A problem arose when we began pair programming: I’m a bottom-up engineer who is content to dive into the muck and dig my way out by trying a lot of things quickly and skimming over the details. Karl, however, is a top-down engineer who wants to get the full lay of the land and dive into the implementation of almost every method on the call stack before proceeding to tackle the bug. This resulted in some epic interpersonal conflicts, disagreements, and the occasional heated argument. It got to the

多年前，我在写一个把 CVS 仓库转换到 Subversion（后来是 Git）的工具。由于 CVS 的种种古怪，我不断挖出离奇的 bug。因为我的老朋友兼同事 Karl 对 CVS 了如指掌，我们决定一起修这些 bug。当我们开始结对编程时，问题来了：我是一个自底向上的工程师，满足于一头扎进泥潭、靠快速试很多东西、略过细节来挖出路；而 Karl 是一个自顶向下的工程师，他想先摸清全貌、深入调用栈上几乎每个方法的实现，然后再去对付 bug。这导致了一些史诗级的人际冲突、分歧，以及偶尔激烈的争吵。它发展到了

原书第 67 页

point at which the two of us simply couldn’t pair-program together: it was too frustrating for us both. That said, we had a longstanding history of trust and respect for each other. Combined with patience, this helped us work out a new method of collaborating. We would sit together at the computer, identify the bug, and then split up and attack the problem from two directions at once (top-down and bottom-up) before coming back together with our findings. Our patience and willingness to improvise new working styles not only saved the project, but also our friendship.

我们俩根本无法再一起结对编程的地步：对我们俩都太挫败了。话虽如此，我们之间有着长久的信任与尊重。再加上耐心，这帮助我们摸索出一种新的协作方式。我们会一起坐在电脑前，定位 bug，然后分头从两个方向（自顶向下与自底向上）同时进攻这个问题，最后再带着各自的发现会合。我们的耐心以及临场发明新工作方式的意愿，不仅挽救了项目，也挽救了我们的友谊。

Be open to influence · 乐于接受影响

The more open you are to influence, the more you are able to influence; the more vulnerable you are, the stronger you appear. These statements sound like bizarre contradictions. But everyone can think of someone they’ve worked with who is just maddeningly stubborn—no matter how much people try to persuade them, they dig their heels in even more. What eventually happens to such team members? In our experience, people stop listening to their opinions or objections; instead, they end up “routing around” them like an obstacle everyone takes for granted. You certainly don’t want to be that person, so keep this idea in your head: it’s OK for someone else to change your mind. In the opening chapter of this book, we said that engineering is inherently about trade-offs. It’s impossible for you to be right about everything all the time unless you have an unchanging environment and perfect knowledge, so of course you should change your mind when presented with new evidence. Choose your battles carefully: to be heard properly, you first need to listen to others. It’s better to do this listening before putting a stake in the ground or firmly announcing a decision—if you’re constantly changing your mind, people will think you’re wishy-washy.

你越乐于接受影响，你就越能影响别人；你越展露脆弱，你显得越强大。这些话听起来像离奇的矛盾。但每个人都能想到某个共事过的、固执得令人抓狂的人——无论别人怎么劝，他反而把脚跟站得更稳。这种团队成员最终会落得什么下场？以我们的经验，人们会不再听他的意见或反对；相反，他们最终会像绕过一个人人习以为常的障碍那样“绕开”他。你当然不想成为那种人，所以把这个念头记在脑子里：让别人改变你的想法，是可以的。在本书开篇那一章里我们说过，工程本质上就是权衡。你不可能在所有时候、所有事情上都正确——除非你拥有一个不变的环境和完美的知识——所以当新证据摆在面前时，你当然应该改变想法。谨慎选择你要打的仗：要被人好好倾听，你首先需要倾听别人。最好是在 stake in the ground、或坚定宣布一个决策之前就先倾听——如果你总是改主意，人们会觉得你没主见。

The idea of vulnerability can seem strange, too. If someone admits ignorance of the topic at hand or the solution to a problem, what sort of credibility will they have in a group? Vulnerability is a show of weakness, and that destroys trust, right? Not true. Admitting that you’ve made a mistake or you’re simply out of your league can increase your status over the long run. In fact, the willingness to express vulnerability is an outward show of humility, it demonstrates accountability and the willingness to take responsibility, and it’s a signal that you trust others’ opinions. In return, people end up respecting your honesty and strength. Sometimes, the best thing you can do is just say, “I don’t know.”

展露脆弱这个想法也可能显得奇怪。如果一个人承认自己对当前话题或某个问题的解法无知，他在群体里还会有什么样的可信度？脆弱是示弱，而那会摧毁信任，对吧？并非如此。承认自己犯了错、或自己确实力有不逮，长期来看反而能提升你的地位。事实上，表达脆弱的意愿是谦逊的外在表现，它展现了担当与承担责任的意愿，也是你信任他人意见的信号。作为回报，人们最终会敬重你的诚实与力量。有时候，你能做的最好的事，就是 simply 说一句“我不知道”。

Professional politicians, for example, are notorious for never admitting error or ignorance, even when it’s patently obvious that they’re wrong or unknowledgeable about a subject. This behavior exists primarily because politicians are constantly under attack by their opponents, and it’s why most people don’t believe a word that politicians say. When you’re writing software, however, you don’t need to be continually on the

例如，职业政客从不承认错误或无知，是出了名的——哪怕他们错了、或对某话题不懂已经昭然若揭。这种行为主要存在，是因为政客不断遭到对手攻击，而这也是为什么大多数人对政客说的话一个字都不信。然而当你在写软件时，你不需要一直处于

defensive—your teammates are collaborators, not competitors. You all have the same goal.

防御姿态——你的队友是协作者，不是竞争者。你们有着同一个目标。

Being Googley · 做“Googley”

At Google, we have our own internal version of the principles of “humility, respect, and trust” when it comes to behavior and human interactions. From the earliest days of our culture, we often referred to actions as being “Googley” or “not Googley.” The word was never explicitly defined; rather, everyone just sort of took it to mean “don’t be evil” or “do the right thing” or “be good to each other.” Over time, people also started using the term “Googley” as an informal test for culture-fit whenever we would interview a candidate for an engineering job, or when writing internal performance reviews of one another. People would often express opinions about others using the term; for example, “the person coded well, but didn’t seem to have a very Googley attitude.”

在 Google，当涉及行为与人际互动时，我们有自己内部版的“谦逊、尊重与信任”原则。从我们文化的最早时期起，我们就常把某些行为称作“Googley”或“不 Googley”。这个词从未被明确定义；相反，大家大致把它理解为“不作恶”“做正确的事”或“彼此善待”。随着时间推移，人们还开始在面试工程岗位候选人、或撰写彼此的内部绩效评估时，把“Googley”当作一种非正式的文化契合度测试。人们常用这个词来表达对他人的看法，例如：“这个人代码写得不错，但态度看起来不太 Googley。”

Of course, we eventually realized that the term “Googley” was being overloaded with meaning; worse yet, it could become a source of unconscious bias in hiring or evaluations. If “Googley” means something different to every employee, we run the risk of the term starting to mean “is just like me.” Obviously, that’s not a good test for hiring—we don’t want to hire people “just like me,” but people from a diverse set of backgrounds and with different opinions and experiences. An interviewer’s personal desire to have a beer with a candidate (or coworker) should never be considered a valid signal about somebody else’s performance or ability to thrive at Google.

当然，我们最终意识到“Googley”这个词被塞进了过多含义；更糟的是，它可能在招聘或评估中成为无意识偏见的来源。如果“Googley”对每个员工意味着不同的东西，我们就面临这个词开始变成“和我一样”的风险。显然，那不是一个好的招聘测试——我们不想招“和我一样”的人，而是来自多元背景、拥有不同观点与经验的人。一位面试官个人想和候选人（或同事）一起喝杯啤酒的愿望，绝不应该被当作关于某人绩效或在 Google 能否成长的有效信号。

Google eventually fixed the problem by explicitly defining a rubric for what we mean by “Googleyness”—a set of attributes and behaviors that we look for that represent strong leadership and exemplify “humility, respect, and trust”:

Google 最终通过明确定义一套“Google 气质（Googleyness）”的评分标准来解决这个问题——它是我们所看重的、代表强大领导力并体现“谦逊、尊重与信任”的一组属性与行为：

  • Thrives in ambiguity: Can deal with conflicting messages or directions, build consensus, and make progress against a problem, even when the environment is constantly shifting.

    在模糊中茁壮成长：即便环境不断变化，也能处理相互冲突的信息或方向、建立共识、推动问题取得进展。

  • Values feedback: Has humility to both receive and give feedback gracefully and understands how valuable feedback is for personal (and team) development.

    重视反馈：有谦逊之心，能优雅地接受和给出反馈，并理解反馈对个人（及团队）发展有多宝贵。

  • Challenges status quo: Is able to set ambitious goals and pursue them even when there might be resistance or inertia from others.

    挑战现状：即便可能遭遇他人的阻力或惰性，也能设定有雄心的目标并去追求。

  • Puts the user first: Has empathy and respect for users of Google’s products and pursues actions that are in their best interests.

    用户第一：对 Google 产品的用户抱有同理心与尊重，并追求符合他们最佳利益的行动。

原书第 69 页

  • Cares about the team: Has empathy and respect for coworkers and actively works to help them without being asked, improving team cohesion.

    关心团队：对同事抱有同理心与尊重，主动在未被要求时帮助他们，提升团队凝聚力。

  • Does the right thing: Has a strong sense of ethics about everything they do; willing to make difficult or inconvenient decisions to protect the integrity of the team and product.

    做正确的事：对所做的一切有强烈的道德感；愿意为保护团队与产品的完整性而做出艰难或不便的决策。

Now that we have these best-practice behaviors better defined, we’ve begun to shy away from using the term “Googley.” It’s always better to be specific about expectations!

既然我们已经把这些最佳实践行为定义得更清楚了，我们就开始避免使用“Googley”这个词。对期望讲得越具体，总是越好！

Conclusion · 结语

The foundation for almost any software endeavor—of almost any size—is a well-functioning team. Although the Genius Myth of the solo software developer still persists, the truth is that no one really goes it alone. For a software organization to stand the test of time, it must have a healthy culture, rooted in humility, trust, and respect that revolves around the team, rather than the individual. Further, the creative nature of software development requires that people take risks and occasionally fail; for people to accept that failure, a healthy team environment must exist.

几乎任何规模的软件事业，其根基都是一支运转良好的团队。尽管孤独软件开发者的天才迷思仍然挥之不去，但真相是：没有谁真的是单打独斗。一个软件组织要想经受时间考验，就必须拥有健康的文化——这种文化植根于谦逊、信任与尊重，并且围绕团队、而不是个人运转。此外，软件开发的创造性本质要求人们承担风险、偶尔失败；而要让人们接受那种失败，就必须存在一个健康的团队环境。

TL;DRs · 要点小结（TL;DR）

  • Be aware of the trade-offs of working in isolation.

    要意识到独自工作的种种权衡。

  • Acknowledge the amount of time that you and your team spend communicating and in interpersonal conflict. A small investment in understanding personalities and working styles of yourself and others can go a long way toward improving productivity.

    承认你和团队花在沟通与人际冲突上的时间。花一点功夫了解自己与他人的性格和工作风格，对提升生产力大有帮助。

  • If you want to work effectively with a team or a large organization, be aware of your preferred working style and that of others.

    如果你想与一个团队或大型组织高效协作，要清楚自己偏好的工作风格，也要清楚他人的工作风格。
